analysis.one_liner: Opens federal lands and coastal waters to oil and gas drilling and blocks EPA climate rules for power plants.
analysis.headline: The House passed this energy bill 226–191 on September 18, 2014, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This was an omnibus energy bill. It would have approved the Keystone XL pipeline by declaring every federal permit already granted, forced fast decisions on natural gas pipeline and LNG export applications, opened more of the outer Continental Shelf and federal lands to oil and gas drilling, and stopped the EPA from carrying out its proposed rules limiting carbon pollution from coal- and gas-fired power plants. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and coal companies gain the most: guaranteed approval of Keystone XL, faster permits with automatic approval if agencies miss deadlines, new offshore lease sales and mandated onshore and oil shale leasing, and the elimination of EPA carbon rules for power plants. LNG exporters get 30-day export decisions. Communities along pipeline routes get some construction jobs, and the bill encourages hiring U.S. workers and using U.S.-made equipment for federal mineral development.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no presidential permit is needed for the Keystone XL pipeline, deems the existing environmental review and Endangered Species and Migratory Bird findings complete, and orders the Army Corps to issue water permits within 90 days — effectively approving the project by law.

Requires federal regulators to approve or deny natural gas pipeline certificates within 12 months, and any other agency's permit within 90 days; if the agency misses the deadline, the permit takes effect automatically.
Directs the Energy Department to decide liquefied natural gas export applications within 30 days after the environmental review concludes, with expedited court review of any delay.

Opens more of the outer Continental Shelf to oil and gas leasing — at least half the unleased acreage in the most resource-rich planning areas, plus mandated sales off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California — and shares 37.5% of new leasing revenue with coastal states.

Sets deadlines for drilling permits on federal land, deems applications approved if the Interior Department misses the deadline, requires annual lease sales in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve, and mandates commercial oil shale lease sales in Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming.

Blocks EPA climate rules for power plants: new standards must be proven already achieved at existing units, rules for existing plants cannot take effect unless Congress sets their effective date, and the social cost of carbon cannot be used in cost-benefit analysis.

analysis.who_pays: People living near new pipeline, drilling, and oil shale development would bear the local environmental and water risks, since the bill deems many reviews complete, shields new lease acreage from protest, charges $5,000 per protest, and makes losing parties in court pay the winners' legal fees. Weakened EPA climate rules leave the public bearing the costs of carbon pollution. Sharing 37.5% of new offshore leasing revenue with coastal states reduces what remains for the federal Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near drilling and all taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill strips out environmental review and public participation: it deems Keystone XL's environmental statements sufficient, shields new lease acreage from protest, charges a $5,000 fee for each protest, requires losing parties in court challenges to pay the winners' legal fees, and shortens filing windows to 60 days.

It nullifies proposed EPA greenhouse gas standards for new, modified, and existing fossil fuel power plants and bars the EPA from using the social cost of carbon unless Congress authorizes it, removing the main federal limits on power plant carbon emissions.
It directs lease sales in areas previously excluded from the federal offshore program, including off Virginia, South Carolina, and Southern California's Santa Maria and Santa Barbara/Ventura basins.
It prohibits federal hydraulic fracturing rules on federal and Indian lands in any state that has its own fracking regulations, deferring to state rules of varying strength.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised faster permitting and more domestic energy, which supporters said would lower prices and create jobs. But the speed-ups were bought by cutting environmental review, limiting public protest, and removing EPA carbon standards, so the main benefits flowed to the companies that would hold the new leases and the utilities relieved of compliance costs, while the costs fell on communities along new pipeline and drilling routes and on everyone exposed to the emissions the blocked rules would have limited. As a legislative matter it also never happened: the House vote produced no law.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it along party lines, but the Senate set it on its calendar without ever voting, and the bill expired when that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 15, 2014, referred to five House committees, and brought to the floor under a closed rule just three days later without a single committee hearing or mark-up.
A Democratic motion to recommit — adding measures to police energy-market speculation and deny expedited permitting to companies releasing toxic petroleum coke air pollutants — failed 193 to 222.
The House passed the bill on September 18, 2014, 226 to 191, with 217 of 232 Republicans in favor and 184 of 199 Democrats opposed.
The Senate received the bill on November 12, 2014, and placed it on its calendar, but no vote ever occurred; the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died there.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, none of the bill's provisions took effect: the expanded offshore and federal-land leasing never happened, and the EPA climate rules the bill would have nullified stayed on the books. Oil, gas, and coal interests gained nothing; the environmental protections it targeted survived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA climate rules and coastal waters stayed protected

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 217 of 232 Republicans voted yes while 184 of 199 Democrats voted no; only 9 Democrats crossed over.

industries.note: The bill approves Keystone XL, mandates new offshore lease sales, speeds onshore drilling permits with automatic approval if deadlines are missed, requires annual leasing in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, mandates oil shale sales, and bars federal fracking rules where states regulate. These provisions transfer access to public lands and waters to leaseholders.

It nullifies proposed EPA greenhouse gas standards for power plants, requires Congress to set effective dates for any future rules covering existing plants, bars use of the social cost of carbon, and mandates reinstatement of the 2008 stream buffer rule in place of stricter versions. This relieves coal companies and coal-burning utilities of the carbon limits the EPA had proposed.

The Energy Department would have to decide export applications within 30 days after the environmental review concludes, with expedited court review of any failure to decide. Exporters waiting in a long queue would move their cargoes to overseas buyers much sooner.

FERC must approve or deny pipeline certificates within 12 months and other agencies within 90 days, with permits taking effect automatically if deadlines are missed. Developers get certainty and speed; landowners and communities along routes get shorter windows to raise objections.

industries.industry: Tribal energy developers (notably the Navajo Nation)
industries.note: The bill lets tribes appraise their own land for energy transactions, authorizes Navajo Nation commercial leases up to 99 years without Interior approval, and exempts Indian trust lands from federal fracking rules without tribal consent. These provisions give tribes more control over energy development on their land.
